q: What is a support vector machine?
short: A classifier that finds the separating hyperplane with the maximum margin to the closest training points of each class.
detail: Margin 2/‖w‖; minimise ½‖w‖² s.t. yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1. Soft margins and kernels extend it to noisy and non-linear data.
example: Spam vs ham with a linear SVM on word counts.
mistakes: Calling any linear classifier an SVM.

q: What are support vectors?
short: The training points lying on (or, with a soft margin, inside) the margin; they have α > 0 and alone determine the hyperplane.
detail: Removing a non-support vector leaves the solution unchanged; w = Σ αᵢyᵢxᵢ over SVs only.
follow: What happens if you delete a support vector?
mistakes: Saying all points nearest the line are SVs regardless of α.

q: Why is the margin 2/‖w‖?
short: With canonical scaling the margin hyperplanes are wᵀx + b = ±1; their distance along the unit normal w/‖w‖ is 2/‖w‖.
follow: Why minimise ½‖w‖² instead of maximising 2/‖w‖?
mistakes: Forgetting the factor 2.

q: What does the C parameter do?
short: It sets the penalty on slack (margin violations): large C → narrow margin, few training errors; small C → wide margin, more errors.
detail: C ≈ 1/λ in hinge + λ‖w‖². Choose by cross-validation; with RBF tune C and γ jointly.
example: : low C misclassifies one blue point.
mistakes: Thinking larger C always generalises better.

q: What is the kernel trick?
short: Replacing every dot product xᵢ·xⱼ in the SVM dual and prediction with K(xᵢ, xⱼ) = φ(xᵢ)·φ(xⱼ), so we work in a high-dimensional space without computing φ.
detail: Possible because the dual depends on data only through dot products. RBF corresponds to an infinite-dimensional φ.
example: (x·z)² equals the dot product of all pairwise products.
mistakes: Saying the trick computes φ(x).

q: Hard margin vs soft margin?
short: Hard margin requires perfect separation (yᵢf(xᵢ) ≥ 1); soft margin adds slack ξᵢ ≥ 0 with cost CΣξᵢ.
detail: Soft-margin dual has box constraints 0 ≤ α ≤ C. Hard margin fails on inseparable data and overfits outliers.
follow: Is hard margin the limit C → ∞?
mistakes: Using hard margin on real data.

q: Name common SVM kernels.
short: Linear xᵀz; polynomial (1 + xᵀz)ᵖ; Gaussian/RBF exp(−‖x − z‖²/2σ²); sigmoid tanh(β₀xᵀz + β₁).
detail: Linear for high-dimensional sparse data; RBF as a strong default for low/medium dimensions; polynomial for interaction features.
example: Ring data needs poly or RBF.
follow: When is the sigmoid kernel invalid?
mistakes: Forgetting to scale features for RBF.

q: SVM vs logistic regression?
short: Same regulariser, different loss: hinge (1 − z)⁺ vs log(1 + e^−z). SVM ignores points beyond the margin; LR rewards every point and outputs probabilities.
detail: SVM is sparse; LR is smooth, gives probabilities and is easier at scale.
mistakes: Claiming SVMs output probabilities.

q: How do SVMs handle multi-class problems?
short: One-vs-all (C classifiers, most confident wins) or one-vs-one (C(C − 1)/2 classifiers, majority vote).
detail: OvA scores 3.5, 6.2, 1.4, 5.5 → class 2; OvO votes 1, 1, 4, 2, 4, 4 → class 4.
mistakes: Saying OvO needs C classifiers.

q: What is the hinge loss?
short: max(0, 1 − y·f(x)): zero for points beyond the margin, linear penalty otherwise.
detail: Convex upper bound on 0-1 loss; non-differentiable at y·f(x) = 1. Equals the optimal slack ξᵢ.
mistakes: Confusing it with the logistic loss.

q: Derive the SVM dual.
short: Lagrangian L = ½‖w‖² − Σαᵢ[yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) − 1]; ∂L/∂w = 0 → w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ; ∂L/∂b = 0 → Σαᵢyᵢ = 0; substitute to get W(α) = Σαᵢ − ½ΣΣαᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼxᵢᵀxⱼ.
detail: Maximise W s.t. αᵢ ≥ 0 and Σαᵢyᵢ = 0 (soft margin: αᵢ ≤ C). Concave QP.
follow: Why is strong duality valid here?
mistakes: Dropping Σαᵢyᵢ = 0.

q: State the KKT conditions and what they imply for SVMs.
short: Stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility (α ≥ 0) and complementary slackness αᵢ[yᵢf(xᵢ) − 1] = 0.
detail: So αᵢ > 0 only for points on the margin; soft margin: αᵢ = 0 outside, 0 < αᵢ < C on the margin, αᵢ = C inside/misclassified.
follow: How is b computed from KKT?
mistakes: Using an α = C point to compute b.

q: Solve the 3-SV example.
short: With augmented vectors, solve −2α₁ + 4α₂ + 4α₃ = −1, −4α₁ + 11α₂ + 9α₃ = 1, −4α₁ + 9α₂ + 11α₃ = 1 → α = (3.5, 0.75, 0.75); w̃ = (0, 1, −2).
detail: Boundary x₂ = 2, margin 2. scikit-learn confirms.
mistakes: Forgetting the label signs.

q: Why does the soft-margin dual have αᵢ ≤ C?
short: From ∂L/∂ξᵢ = C − αᵢ − μᵢ = 0 with μᵢ ≥ 0 (the multiplier for ξᵢ ≥ 0), so αᵢ = C − μᵢ ≤ C.
detail: The slack variables vanish from the dual; only the box changes.
mistakes: Thinking ξ appears in the dual objective.

q: Show that (1 + xᵀz)² is a valid kernel in 2-D.
short: Expand to 1 + x₁²z₁² + 2x₁x₂z₁z₂ + x₂²z₂² + 2x₁z₁ + 2x₂z₂ = Φ(x)ᵀΦ(z) with Φ(x) = (1, x₁², √2x₁x₂, x₂², √2x₁, √2x₂).
detail: An explicit feature map proves PSD-ness.
follow: What dimension for degree p in d inputs?
mistakes: Dropping the √2 factors.

q: What makes a function a valid (Mercer) kernel?
short: Symmetric and positive semi-definite: every Gram matrix satisfies cᵀKc ≥ 0.
detail: Closure: αk, k + α (α > 0), k₁ + k₂, k₁k₂, f(x)k(x,z)f(z), exp(k) are kernels.
follow: Why does PSD matter for the optimiser?
mistakes: Using an arbitrary similarity as a kernel.

q: How do γ and C interact in an RBF SVM?
short: γ = 1/2σ² sets how local each SV's influence is; C sets the penalty on violations. Large γ + large C → overfitting islands; small γ + small C → near-linear underfit.
detail: Grid-search on a log scale with CV, after standardising features.
mistakes: Tuning C with γ fixed at a bad value.

q: Your RBF SVM has 95% of training points as support vectors. What does that tell you?
short: The model is barely compressing the data: classes overlap heavily, C is small, γ is too large, or features are unscaled/uninformative.
detail: LOO error ≤ #SV/n hints at poor generalisation; check scaling, tune C/γ, engineer features.
mistakes: Celebrating many SVs as 'more information'.

q: How is b computed after solving the dual?
short: For any support vector with 0 < αₖ < C, b = yₖ − Σαᵢyᵢ K(xᵢ, xₖ); average over all such vectors for numerical stability.
detail: Points with α = C can't be used (they have ξ > 0).
mistakes: Using a non-SV point.

q: Large dataset (10M rows, 300 features). Would you use a kernel SVM?
short: Usually not: kernel SVMs need O(n²) kernel values and O(n²–n³) time. Use a linear SVM (liblinear/SGD), logistic regression, gradient boosting, or approximate kernels (random Fourier features, Nyström).
detail: Linear SVM training is O(nd) per epoch.
mistakes: Running SVC(kernel='rbf') on 10M rows.

q: Why does a convex QP guarantee a unique solution for SVMs?
short: ½‖w‖² is strictly convex in w and the constraints are linear, so the feasible set is convex and w* is unique (b unique except degenerate cases).
detail: The dual is concave (PSD Gram matrix); α may not be unique but w is.
mistakes: Confusing uniqueness of w with uniqueness of α.

q: How does SMO work?
short: Sequential Minimal Optimisation updates two α's at a time (the minimum that keeps Σαᵢyᵢ = 0), solving each 2-variable QP analytically with clipping to [L, H].
detail: Choose pairs violating KKT; update b; repeat until KKT within tolerance. Memory O(n) without storing the full Gram matrix.
mistakes: Updating a single α and breaking the equality constraint.

q: What is the representer theorem and how does it relate to SVMs?
short: For regularised loss minimisation in an RKHS, the minimiser is f(x) = Σαᵢ K(xᵢ, x): a combination of kernels at training points.
detail: Explains why the SVM solution is expressed through training points; sparsity comes from hinge loss.
mistakes: Thinking only SVMs use kernels.

q: How do you get probabilities from an SVM?
short: Platt scaling: fit a sigmoid P(y = 1|f) = 1/(1 + exp(Af + B)) on held-out decision values; or isotonic regression.
detail: Must use CV/held-out data to avoid overfit; scikit-learn SVC(probability=True) does internal 5-fold.
mistakes: Treating |f(x)| as a probability.

q: Explain ε-insensitive support vector regression.
short: SVR fits f with a tube of width ε: errors within ε cost nothing; beyond, linear penalty C·(|y − f| − ε). Minimise ½‖w‖² + CΣ(ξ + ξ*).
detail: Same dual/kernel machinery; support vectors are points on or outside the tube.
example: Predicting cell traffic with an RBF SVR.
mistakes: Using classification hinge loss for regression.

q: Why is the Gaussian kernel's feature space infinite-dimensional?
short: exp(−γ‖x − z‖²) = exp(−γ‖x‖²)exp(−γ‖z‖²)exp(2γxᵀz), and the Taylor series of exp(2γxᵀz) contains polynomial kernels of every degree.
detail: So any finite dataset is separable with small enough σ: hence the overfitting risk.
follow: Is the RBF Gram matrix always full rank?
mistakes: Saying RBF maps to n dimensions.

q: Hinge loss is not differentiable; how is a linear SVM trained with SGD?
short: Use the subgradient: for y·f < 1, ∇ = λw − yx; otherwise λw (Pegasos).
detail: Pegasos converges in Õ(1/(λε)) iterations independent of n.
mistakes: Using the logistic gradient by mistake.

q: Classes are 99:1 imbalanced. How do you adapt the SVM?
short: Use class weights (different C per class, C₊ = C·n₋/n₊), tune the threshold on the decision function, evaluate with PR-AUC/recall.
detail: Unweighted SVM tends to sacrifice the minority class as its errors are cheap overall.
mistakes: Reporting accuracy only.

q: Why is folding the bias into w (augmented vectors) not exactly the standard SVM?
short: Then ‖w̃‖² = ‖w‖² + b², so the bias is regularised and the constraint Σαᵢyᵢ = 0 disappears; the solution can differ from the true max-margin hyperplane.
detail: In the examples it happens to coincide (ex. 1) or gives the correct direction after rescaling (Example-1).
mistakes: Assuming the shortcut always gives the max margin.

q: One-vs-one or one-vs-all for SVMs?
short: OvO trains C(C − 1)/2 small problems (often faster overall for kernel SVMs since cost is superlinear in n) and avoids imbalance; OvA trains C large imbalanced problems with uncalibrated scores.
detail: Both can leave ambiguous regions; Crammer–Singer is a joint multi-class SVM.
example: libsvm uses OvO; liblinear uses OvA.
mistakes: Thinking OvO is always slower because it has more models.
